analysis.one_liner: Strips the consumer financial bureau of its power to restrict forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-paragraph bill would repeal section 1028 of the Dodd-Frank law, the provision that lets the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau restrict or condition mandatory arbitration clauses in contracts for credit cards, bank accounts, loans, and other financial products [S2][S3]. Financial companies routinely write such clauses into their contracts, requiring customers to settle disputes in private arbitration and blocking them from banding together in class-action lawsuits. The bill never moved past its committee referral and expired with the Congress [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Financial firms that use forced arbitration clauses — credit card issuers, lenders, payday lenders, debt collectors, and other financial product providers. Repealing the CFPB's authority under section 1028 would remove the legal threat to those clauses, letting firms keep directing consumer disputes into a private process where outcomes are typically not public and class-action relief is unavailable [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card issuers, lenders, and debt collectors

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 1028 of the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, which authorizes the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection to restrict the use of arbitration agreements between financial providers and consumers [S2][S3].
The bill is a single operative clause plus a clerical amendment to Dodd-Frank's table of contents — it only removes the regulator's authority and creates no replacement consumer remedy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers of financial products. Without the CFPB's authority to restrict arbitration, customers could be required to take disputes — billing errors, unlawful fees, discrimination claims — to an arbitrator chosen under the company's contract terms, rather than joining a class action where one person's case can win relief for thousands of similarly situated customers. Consumers who banked on a future CFPB arbitration restriction would bear the cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers disputing financial-product fees and practices

drawbacks.text: Supporters of arbitration clauses argue that individual arbitration can be faster and cheaper for an aggrieved consumer than years of class-action litigation, and that class actions sometimes deliver small recoveries to class members while paying large fees to lawyers — a fairness argument the bill implicitly relies on by leaving arbitration in place [S3].

The bill is purely subtractive: it repeals the CFPB's authority without creating any alternative safeguard, so nothing would replace the class-action channel that arbitration clauses typically block [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit flows entirely to financial firms that want to keep forced arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in their contracts; its cost falls on consumers whose disputes with those firms would stay in private, non-public arbitration. With zero cosponsors and no committee action, it was a statement of position more than a working bill [S4][S5].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2016 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Marlin Stutzman introduced the bill on June 22, 2016 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day and never advanced further [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: because the bill died, the CFPB's authority to restrict forced arbitration remained on the books, so consumers kept the (unused at the time) statutory protection while financial firms faced no new restriction either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms kept forced arbitration untouched

for.name: Rep. Marlin Stutzman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee on his motion; he took no further recorded action on it.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died without a recorded vote, so no roll call shows the split [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Consumer financial services (credit card issuers, banks, lenders, debt collectors)
industries.note: The bill would remove the statutory basis for the CFPB to restrict mandatory arbitration clauses, letting these firms keep steering customer disputes into private arbitration and blocking class actions [S2][S3]. Ordinary consumers lose a potential route to collective relief when the firms win.
Repealing section 1028 would delete an enforcement-adjacent tool the CFPB could have used against arbitration clauses that curb consumer access to court [S2][S3].
